Ground state phases of the two-dimension electron gas with a unified variational approach

August 24, 2026
Abstract

The two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) is a fundamental model, which is drawing increasing interest because of recent advances in experimental and theoretical studies of 2D materials. Current understanding of the ground state of the 2DEG relies on quantum Monte Carlo calculations, based on variational comparisons of different ansatze for different phases. We use a single variational ansatz, a general backflow-type wave function using a message-passing neural quantum state architecture, for a unified description across the entire density range. The variational optimization consistently leads to lower ground-state energies than previous best results. Transition into a Wigner crystal (WC) phase occurs automatically at rs=37±1r_{s}=37\pm 1, a density lower than currently believed. Between the liquid and WC phases, the same ansatz and variational search strongly suggest the existence of intermediate states in a broad range of densities, with enhanced short-range nematic spin correlations.

The uniform electron gas, also known as jellium, has been one of the most important fundamental models in condensed matter physics. The ground-state energies computed in jellium [1, 2, 3, 4] also serve as the foundation for density functionals which are widely applied in ab initio computations in many disciplines. Recently the two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) has drawn renewed interest owing to the many recent experimental discoveries in two-dimensional materials [5, 6, 7, 8, 9]. Despite the simplicity of the model, the phase diagram of jellium is not fully understood. Theoretically, a variety of candidate ground states have been proposed [10], including theory of microemulsion [11] and metalic electron crystal [12] between phase transitions. Computationally, the most accurate studies have confirmed only a Fermi liquid (FL) phase at high density, and a Wigner crystal (WC) phase (possibly with different spin polarizations) at low density, with a transition between them estimated at rs=31±1r_{s}=31\pm 1 in two dimensions, based on the most accurate computations to date [4]. Experimentally, generalized WC phases, in the presence of external potentials, have been detected [13, 14, 15], and higher density regimes are being realized and studied. In particular, a low-temperature magneto-optical experiment in MoSe2 [16] reported evidence for a liquid phase with enhanced spin susceptibility and a microemulsion phase in between the WC and the FL.

The primary challenge in computationally determining the ground-state phases in jellium is that candidate states are separated by extremely small energy differences. In order to make further progress, we need methods that have systematically improvable and, possibly more importantly, balanced accuracy across different regimes. Quantum Monte Carlo calculations have been the standard tool used so far. However, they typically rely on different variational ansatze for different phases. The ground state at each density is determined by comparing the computed energies from each candidate ansatz, and the search for different states is limited by the expressiveness of the variational ansatze that can be computed given the available resources.

Recently, neural network wavefunctions [17, 18, 19, 20], also known as neural quantum states (NQS), have been used as ansatze in variational Monte Carlo (VMC) calculations. They significantly expand the expressiveness of the variational wave functions that can be explored and computed. Many developments and applications have shown the promise of this approach. Impressive accuracy has been achieved in a variety of benchmark studies in fermion systems. However, to date, few applications in this area have demonstrated the potential predictive power that can lead to physical results or insights beyond the reach of existing capabilities.

In this paper, we leverage NQS to study the ground state phases of the 2DEG. We uncover evidence of short-range nematic spin correlations in a broad range of intermediate densities, and automatically discover a “floating” WC. Building on an ansatz of Slater-Jastrow-backflow form with message-passing graph neural network components [21], we introduce multiple planewaves (MPs) into each orbital, allowing the ansatz to span both the liquid and WC phases. Using this single ansatz, which we call (MP)2NQS, we obtain variational ground-state energies significantly lower than those from state-of-the-art QMC [4]. The transition to the WC is automatic, yielding a lower critical density (rs=37±1r_{s}=37\pm 1) than previously believed. In the WC phase, the ansatz yields a “floating” crystal with partially restored translational symmetry. With the same ansatz, our calculations suggest the existence of an intermediate state in a wide range of densities (rs∼10r_{s}\sim 10-3535) before the WC transition, a liquid state with enhanced short-range spin correlations which break rotational symmetry. Although the calculations are still in modest system sizes (but comparable to the largest sizes that have been treated by NQS), our analysis indicates that the nematic spin correlation is quite robust, and that the 2DEG may have much new physics to offer.

The 2DEG consists of interacting electrons in a uniform compensating charge background. The Hamiltonian (in Hartree atomic units)

H=−12∑i∇i2+∑i<j1|𝒓i−𝒓j|+b.g.H=-\dfrac{1}{2}\sum\limits_{i}\nabla_{i}^{2}+\sum\limits_{i<j}\dfrac{1}{|\boldsymbol{r}_{i}-\boldsymbol{r}_{j}|}+{\rm b.g.} (1)

is specified by a single dimensionless parameter, rsr_{s}, the Wigner-Seitz radius in units of the Bohr radius aBa_{\mathrm{B}} (see considerations of a finite simulation with periodic boundary conditions in SM). Our (MP)2NQS ansatz has Slater-Jastrow-backflow form

Ψ(R)=det[{⟨𝒙j;σj|ϕa;χa⟩}]exp⁡(U2​(R)+𝒰​(R)),\Psi(R)=\text{det}\left[\{\langle\boldsymbol{x}_{j};\sigma_{j}|\phi_{a};\chi_{a}\rangle\}\right]\exp\big( U_2(R)+\mathcal{U}(R) \big)\,, (2)

where R≡{𝒓1;σ1;𝒓2;σ2;⋯;𝒓N;σN}R\equiv\{\boldsymbol{r}_{1};\sigma_{1};\boldsymbol{r}_{2};\sigma_{2};\cdots;\boldsymbol{r}_{N};\sigma_{N}\} denotes the coordinates and spins of the NN electrons in the simulation cell of area Ω\Omega (π​rs2=Ω/N\pi r_{s}^{2}=\Omega/N), and the “quasi-particle” coordinates are

𝒙j≡𝒓j+𝒩⁡(R).\boldsymbol{x}_{j}\equiv\boldsymbol{r}_{j}+\mathcal{N}(R)\,. (3)

Both 𝒩\mathcal{N} in Eq. (3) and 𝒰\mathcal{U} in the Jastrow in Eq. (2) are many-body neural network functions, inspired by the message-passing neural quantum states (MP-NQS) ansatz [22]. In this work, we restrict the system to total Sz=0S_{z}=0, and each σj\sigma_{j} is fixed (+1+1 or −1-1). We also keep each orbital χa\chi_{a} as an s^z\hat{s}_{z} eigenstate. (This reduces the Slater determinant to a product of separate spin-↑\uparrow and spin-↓\downarrow components.) Each of the NN orbitals in the Slater determinant can be written as

ϕa​(𝒙)=∑k=1Nkca​k​exp⁡(i​𝑮k⋅𝒙)\phi_{a}(\boldsymbol{x})=\sum_{k=1}^{N_{k}}c_{ak}\exp(\mathrm{i}\bs{G}_k\cdot\bs{x})\, (4)

where {ca​k}\{c_{ak}\} are variational parameters and we choose Nk≫NN_{k}\gg N (multiple planewaves). The function U2U_{2} in Eq. (2) is a sum of isotropic two-body correlators: U2​(R)=∑j≠luσj​σl​(𝒙j−𝒙l)U_{2}(R)=\sum_{j\neq l}u_{\sigma_{j}\sigma_{l}}(\boldsymbol{x}_{j}-\boldsymbol{x}_{l}) , where u+1u_{+1} and u−1u_{-1} are standard functions satisfying the cusp condition for same and opposite spins, respectively [23].

While the original idea of backflow was based on physical intuition from liquid helium [24, 25] and perturbation theory [26, 27, 28], recent implementations [29, 18, 30, 21, 31] parameterize a general all-body, instead of few-body, coordinate transformation. In this work, we adapt the message passing network from [22] as our many-body backflow transformation 𝒩⁡(R)\mathcal{N}(R), with modifications to facilitate optimization. We introduce an extra term 𝒰⁡(R)\mathcal{U}(R) in the Jastrow factor that shares the same message-passing layers with the backflow 𝒩\mathcal{N}, to further improve the expressivity of the ansatz. Details of our implementation can be found in the Supplementary Materials.

We variationally minimize the total energy

E=∫[H​Ψ​(R)/Ψ⁡(R)]​|Ψ⁡(R)|2​𝑑R∫|Ψ⁡(R)|2​𝑑R.E=\frac{\int[H\Psi(R)/\Psi(R)]\,|\Psi(R)|^{2}\,dR}{\int|\Psi(R)|^{2}\,dR}\,. (5)

The Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm (MALA)  [32] is employed to sample electron configurations {R}\{R\} from the unnormalized distribution |Ψ⁡(R)|2|\Psi(R)|^{2}, which allows the evaluation of Eq. (5) as the expectation of the local energy: 𝔼⁡[H​Ψ​(R)/Ψ⁡(R)]\mathbb{E}[H\Psi(R)/\Psi(R)]. New configurations in the Markov chain are proposed using overdamped Langevin dynamics, which utilizes gradient information to increase the acceptance rate. The step size of the Langevin dynamics is adaptively tuned during the optimization according to the average acceptance rate. The optimization of the parameters is performed using the stochastic reconfiguration (SR) method [33, 34] with recently introduced modifications [35] to stabilize and accelerate the process.

We apply the same ansatz and optimization procedure to different rsr_{s} values spanning both liquid and crystal phases. The hyperparameters used for different rsr_{s} values are the same, except for the initial learning rates, which are tuned for each rsr_{s} to account for the different energy scales. The calculations are primarily carried out with N=56N=56 electrons under periodic boundary conditions, with spot checks using N=58N=58 (square simulation cell) and N=120N=120.

The (MP)2NQS ansatz automatically and accurately discovers the WC transition by variational optimization. Our current knowledge of this transition is based on diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) calculations using different VMC ansatze, as shown in Fig. 1. The reference DMC calculations [36] are performed in identical systems as in the (MP)2NQS calculations and obtained with Slater-Jastrow-backflow trial wavefunctions with short-range isotropic two-body correlators, using planewaves for the FL phase and Gaussians for the WC phase.

The optimized variational energy from our neural network ansatz yields a single equation of state line shown in the main plot in Fig. 1, which is lower than that of DMC at all densities. The difference in energies is especially prominent in the liquid phase. In the bottom panel of Fig. 1, we can see the crystallinity of the (MP)2NQS ansatz spontaneously increase across the WC transition. Near the transition, in the range rs∈(34,40)r_{s}\in(34,40), the ansatz discovers states with and without charge order in a narrow energy window depending on the randomly generated initial parameters. The shaded region encapsulates results of all states having energy close to the lowest state (with a threshold of 0.01%0.01\% of the total energy). To locate the critical rsr_{s} more precisely, we use the transfer learning technique to preserve the character (FL or WC) of the ansatz in the transition region and calculate its variational energy. As shown in the inset of Fig. 1, we transferred the liquid state found at rs=36r_{s}=36 up to 3838 and the crystal state found at rs=38r_{s}=38 down to rs=36r_{s}=36. The energy crossing gives a transition point of rs=36.5r_{s}=36.5. After applying finite-size corrections using energies from DMC [4] (which is less costly to run for larger simulation sizes), we obtain an estimated critical value for the WC transition: rs=37±1r_{s}=37\pm 1.

The main advantage of the (MP)2NQS is that, within the same ansatz, correlated phases such as the WC can be automatically discovered. Further, once an NQS has been optimized, many physical observables can be calculated to high precision to characterize the discovered phase. DMC has been the standard for accurate characterization of ground-state properties in jellium. There have been years of sophisticated development and optimization since the early landmark calculation [1]. That the variational energy is lower than DMC is important, not so much for the quantitative improvement, but as a strong indication of the quality of the (MP)2NQS wave function.

We next examine the properties of the (MP)2NQS ground state as a function of rsr_{s}. We compute spin-resolved one- and two-body density functions: ρα​(𝒓)=⟨Ψ|ρ^α​(𝒓)|Ψ⟩\rho_{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r})=\langle\Psi|\hat{\rho}_{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r})|\Psi\rangle and ρ2α,β​(𝒓,𝒓′)=⟨Ψ|ρ^α​(𝒓)​ρ^β​(𝒓′)|Ψ⟩\rho^{\alpha,\beta}_{2}(\boldsymbol{r},\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime})=\langle\Psi|\hat{\rho}_{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r})\hat{\rho}_{\beta}(\boldsymbol{r}^{\prime})|\Psi\rangle, where α\alpha and β\beta are spin indices (∈{↑,↓}\in\Bqty{\uparrow, \downarrow}) and ρ^α​(𝒓)\hat{\rho}_{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r}) is the density operator at 𝒓\boldsymbol{r} for spin α\alpha. The uniform pair correlation function is

g~(𝒓)=ΩN⁡(N−1)∫d𝒓0∑α,β∈{↑,↓}ρ2α,β(𝒓0,𝒓0+𝒓),\tilde{g}(\boldsymbol{r})=\frac{\Omega}{N(N-1)}\int\differential{\bs{r}_0}\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}}\rho^{\alpha,\beta}_{2}(\boldsymbol{r}_{0},\boldsymbol{r}_{0}+\boldsymbol{r})\,, (6)

and the Fourier transform of g~​(𝒓)\tilde{g}(\boldsymbol{r}) is the structure factor

S⁡(𝒌)=\displaystyle S(\boldsymbol{k})= 1+N−1Ω∫d𝒓e−i𝒌⋅𝒓(g~(𝒓)−1).\displaystyle~1+\frac{N-1}{\Omega}\int\differential{\bs{r}}e^{-\mathrm{i}\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}(\tilde{g}(\boldsymbol{r})-1)\,. (7)

Figure 2(a) and (b) show g~​(𝒓)\tilde{g}(\boldsymbol{r}) and S⁡(𝒌)S(\boldsymbol{k}) in direct and reciprocal space, respectively. At rs=40r_{s}=40, g~​(r)\tilde{g}(r) shows strong and persistent oscillation at large distances, indicative of long-range correlation. Correspondingly, the S⁡(𝒌)S(\boldsymbol{k}) exhibits Bragg peaks at wave vectors consistent with a triangular WC. As shown in Fig. 2(b) and the bottom panel of Fig. 1, we find S⁡(𝒌)S(\boldsymbol{k}) is smooth vs. k≡|𝒌|k\equiv|\boldsymbol{k}| for rs≤34r_{s}\leq 34, confirming the lack of long-range charge correlation, and the character of a liquid.

The WC phase discovered by (MP)2NQS exhibits a partially floating nature, characterized by nearly uniform density along the spin stripes of an anti-ferromagnetic (AFM) pattern, as shown in appendix Fig. S3(d). (The broken symmetry spin stripe pattern is built into the ansatz, because we restrict it to colinear spins with fixed σj\sigma_{j} and χ\chi in Eq. (2).) This is different from the usual WC state studied computationally in the 2DEG, in which a WC is assumed and the electron locations in the crystal are specified a priori. This “floating crystal” state, despite being theoretically predicted long ago [37, 38], has not been observed in numerical simulations reported in the literature to the best of our knowledge.

One of the long-standing questions on the electron gas is whether there are intermediate states between the FL and WC and, if so, of what character. The (MP)2NQS provides a unique opportunity to explore this question, given that the ansatz does not require postulating the candidate phases and that it is capable of high accuracy across the density regimes, as the results above indicate. Below, we investigate the ground state from (MP)2NQS more closely at the intermediate densities. We compute the spin-spin correlation function defined as

gs(𝒓)=∑α,β∈{↑,↓}(2δα​β−1)gα​β(𝒓),\displaystyle g_{s}(\boldsymbol{r})=\sum_{\alpha,\beta\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}}(2\delta_{\alpha\beta}-1)g_{\alpha\beta}(\boldsymbol{r}), (8)

where gα​β​(𝒓)g_{\alpha\beta}(\boldsymbol{r}) is the pair correlation function ρ2α,β​(𝒓0,𝒓0+𝒓)/[ρα​(𝒓0)​ρβ​(𝒓0+𝒓)]\rho^{\alpha,\beta}_{2}(\boldsymbol{r}_{0},\boldsymbol{r}_{0}+\boldsymbol{r})/[\rho_{\alpha}(\boldsymbol{r}_{0})\rho_{\beta}(\boldsymbol{r}_{0}+\boldsymbol{r})] after averaging with respect to the reference position 𝒓0\boldsymbol{r}_{0} (as done in Eq. (6)).

We find a strong tendency for short-range anisotropic spin correlations in a wide range of intermediate densities, which we will refer to below as nematic spin correlated liquid (NSCL, for short). In a typical liquid at rs=5r_{s}=5, gs​(𝒓)g_{s}(\boldsymbol{r}) exhibits isotropic short-range AFM correlation due to exchange effects, as shown in Fig. 3(b) and the gray line in Fig. 3(a). In a typical crystal at rs=45r_{s}=45, gs​(𝒓)g_{s}(\boldsymbol{r}) has long-range AFM correlation commensurate with the triangular lattice as shown in Fig. 3(c) (note stripe structure due to restricting to colinear spins, as discussed earlier) and the dot-dashed line in Fig. 3(a). As the interaction strength rsr_{s} increases in the liquid phase, the spin channel develops nematic correlation while the charge channel remains isotropic (Fig. S4). The spin correlation remains very short-ranged until the WC is reached; however, starting from rs∼10r_{s}\sim 10, a preferential AFM direction emerges. The AFM correlation strengthens along this direction and weakens perpendicular to it. With N=56N=56, the simulation cell is rectangular, and almost all of the NSCL found here picked a direction within 10∘10^{\circ} of the short axis. We have also verified with calculations in the N=58N=58 square cell, where the AFM is equally likely to be along the xx- or yy-direction, and the gs​(𝒓)g_{s}(\boldsymbol{r}) is quantitatively consistent with those in Fig. 3(a) (see appendix Figs. S2 and S6). By following the first dip in gs​(r)g_{s}(r) along the preferred direction, which is aligned to yy in Fig. 3(a), we see that the characteristic length of this correlation increases from ∼1.5​rs\sim 1.5\,r_{s} at rs=10r_{s}=10 to ∼1.7​rs\sim 1.7\,r_{s} around the WC transition, as shown in the inset in panel a. This is consistent with the projection of the nearest neighbor distance in the WC along the yy direction (panel c). Therefore, the NSCL connects spin features of the liquid to that of the WC.

We also observed faint spin density stripes in the NSCL. As shown in Fig. 3(e), the six lowest-energy states found at rs=34r_{s}=34 (within 0.01%0.01\% in variational energy) all show some spin density wave order. The six states have spin densities, s⁡(𝒓)≡ρ↑​(𝒓)−ρ↓​(𝒓)s(\boldsymbol{r})\equiv\rho_{\uparrow}(\boldsymbol{r})-\rho_{\downarrow}(\boldsymbol{r}), which vary in pattern, orientation, and strength. However they all have gs​(𝒓)g_{s}(\boldsymbol{r}) nearly identical to Fig. 3(d), oriented in the direction of the AFM stripes. The spin density waves in the two lowest-energy states at rs=34r_{s}=34 have twice the wavelength of the WC. Strictly speaking, the broken symmetry in a one-body observable here is artificial, as we discussed earlier in connection with the partially floating crystals. We interpret these spin density waves as originating from the anisotropic two-body spin correlation, but pinned to a one-body density, possibly by a rough optimization landscape. The charge density remains nearly uniform in the NSCL (Fig. S3). At rs=34r_{s}=34, all the low-energy states we find are liquids. In contrast, at rs=35r_{s}=35, there are some local minima with WC character very close in energy to the lowest-energy state, which is a liquid (Fig. S1). Whether this can be a manifestation of microemulsion [11] in the small simulation cells is an interesting question to explore. In principle, the current ansatz allows this and the possible existence of a metallic electronic crystal to be studied. As shown in Fig. 3(a), the short-range AFM feature is fully developed by rs=15r_{s}=15 and persists all the way up to crystallization. Interestingly, the density range coincides with the recent experimental observation [16] of an intermediate liquid state with high spin susceptibility.

In summary, we report several advances in characterizing and understanding the ground state of the 2DEG, using a neural quantum state ansatz, (MP)2NQS. The single ansatz yields variational energies which are significantly lower than the current state-of-the-art from DMC projections of separately optimized VMC wave functions. It allows a unified description of the 2DEG, finding the FL and WC phases without any a priori specification, and revising the transition to the WC to a lower density than currently assumed. The same variational ansatz suggests the existence of a correlated liquid state with short-range nematic spin correlations at a wide range of intermediate densities. Further studies are needed, for example with more systematic investigation of finite-size effects and more extensive quantification of the different correlations and spin response, in order to better characterize these states and understand their connection with the experimental observations. But these results from the (MP)2NQS already provide evidence and interesting clue that there is rich physics between the FL and WC phases in the electron gas.

Note added: During the preparation of this manuscript, Azadi et al. [39] reported improved DMC calculations in the liquid phase, and a revised transition density of rs=35±1r_{s}=35\pm 1, more consistent with our result.

Ground state phases of the two-dimension electron gas
with a unified variational approach

I.1 Total Energy and Static Structure Factor

In Table 1, we provide the lowest total energies and corresponding S⁡(k)S(k) Bragg peaks obtained using the (MP)2NQS ansatz along with total energies of reference DMC calculations. To emphasize the variation of final states from the frustrated optimization landscape, we show two figures of merit, the energy and averaged Bragg peaks of the structure factor S⁡(k)S(k), in Fig. S1. We find many competitive states in the region rs∈[34,40)r_{s}\in[34,40), depicted both in the energetics and the variety of S⁡(k)S(k) Bragg peak values. The lowest energy states in this regime are all liquid like until rs=38r_{s}=38, but the optimization may find a crystal or stripe state nearby in energy. Not pictured, there are non-crystalline states found at rs≥40r_{s}\geq 40 but they are significantly higher than energy, a factor of approximately 3 higher. We note that the Wigner crystal states with slightly higher energies still show no signs of defects. They may have small modulations in the densities and are not as “floating” as the lowest energy ones.

I.2 Evolution of the AFM Correlations

In Fig. S2, we explore the peak of the gs​(𝒓)g_{s}(\boldsymbol{r}) location as a function of rsr_{s} which was originally shown in the linecut of Fig. 3(c). The peak location roughly represents the distance between two pairs of opposite spin electrons, or the AFM characteristic length ℓ\ell. To obtain the peak location, we fit the underlying histogram data to a Gaussian

G⁡(r,θ,{ℓ,θi,σr,σθ,A,B})=A​exp⁡(−(r−ℓ)2σr2−(θ−θo)2σθ2)+BG(r,\theta;\{\ell,\theta_{i},\sigma_{r},\sigma_{\theta},A,B\})=A\exp\left(-\dfrac{(r-\ell)^{2}}{\sigma_{r}^{2}}-\dfrac{(\theta-\theta_{o})^{2}}{\sigma_{\theta}^{2}}\right)+B (9)

to mitigate bias from finite grid resolution and statistical noise. As rsr_{s} increases, the value of ℓ/rs\ell/r_{s} slowly climbs until gs​(r)g_{s}(r) abruptly changes when the system becomes a WC at sufficiently large rsr_{s}.

We also measure the peak location of the triangular WC along the AFM direction (y axis in the simulation cell). The peak location is determined by a spline fit for the data on the grid along that axis. The average measured peak distance for WC is ℓ/rs≈1.70\ell/r_{s}\approx 1.70, as shown in the dotted horizontal line in Fig. S2. This value is slightly larger than what is predicted from a perfect triangular lattice, 32×2​π3≈1.65\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\times\sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}}\approx 1.65, since the correlation function is distorted locally by the exchange effects.

We also note that the peak distance we get for rs=35r_{s}=35 and 3636 are slightly higher than the averaged crystal value, by around 2 %. One potential cause for this small overshoot is the frustrated optimization landscape, since we have multiple competing local minima of different phases within a small energy range at these two rsr_{s} (see Fig. S1). Whether there is some physical explanation (such as microemulsion) behind this phenomenon is a direction to explore in the future.

I.3 Evolution of observables

We show in this section, for various rsr_{s}, charge and spin densities in Fig. S3, charge and spin correlation functions in Fig. S4, and momentum distributions

n(𝒌)=1N​(2​π)2∫d𝒓0∫d𝒓e−i𝒌⋅𝒓ρ2(𝒓0,𝒓0+𝒓)n(\boldsymbol{k})=\dfrac{1}{N(2\pi)^{2}}\int d\boldsymbol{r}_{0}\int d\boldsymbol{r}e^{-i\boldsymbol{k}\cdot\boldsymbol{r}}\rho_{2}(\boldsymbol{r}_{0},\boldsymbol{r}_{0}+\boldsymbol{r}) (10)

in Fig. S5. The charge density remains uniform in the liquid, whereas the spin density shows faint spin stripes in the NSCL states. The charge correlation remains isotropic in the liquid, where as the spin correlation shows short-range nematic AFM correlation in the NSCL states. The charge momentum distribution appears isotropic with a discontinuity at the Fermi surface k=2/rsk=\sqrt{2}/r_{s} in the liquid. The magnitude of the discontinuity decreases as rsr_{s} increases and disappears in the WC phase.

I.4 Anisotropy Observed in Square Simulation Cells

In the main text, the rectangular simulation cell with N=56N=56 electrons is constructed to be commensurate with a triangular lattice, which could potentially induce an anisotropy in gs​(r)g_{s}(r) and the one-body density patterns. To ensure the observed anisotropy is not an artifact of this cell choice, we also optimize the (MP)2NQS ansatz in a square cell with N=58N=58 electrons. A Wigner crystal is frustrated in a square cell, but similar anisotropy in gs​(r)g_{s}(r) and the one-body density patterns as we approach rsr_{s} of 35 can be seen in Fig. S6.

I.5 Hamiltonian Details

The jellium Hamiltonian for NN electrons with mass mm in a uniform dielectric environment with constant ϵ\epsilon is

H=ℏ22​m​∑i=1N∇i2+e24​π​ϵ​VE,H=\dfrac{\hbar^{2}}{2m}\sum\limits_{i=1}^{N}\nabla_{i}^{2}+\dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon}V_{E}, (11)

where VEV_{E} denotes the interaction energy:

VE=∑i=1N∑j=i+1N∑𝑳s1|𝒓i−𝒓j−𝑳s|+b.g.≡∑i=1N∑j=i+1NvE​(𝒓i−𝒓j)+12​N​vM,V_{E}=\sum\limits_{i=1}^{N}\sum\limits_{j=i+1}^{N}\sum\limits_{\boldsymbol{L}_{s}}\dfrac{1}{|\boldsymbol{r}_{i}-\boldsymbol{r}_{j}-\boldsymbol{L}_{s}|}+b.g.\equiv\sum\limits_{i=1}^{N}\sum\limits_{j=i+1}^{N}v_{E}(\boldsymbol{r}_{i}-\boldsymbol{r}_{j})+\dfrac{1}{2}Nv_{M}, (12)

where 𝑳s\boldsymbol{L}_{s} is the Bravais lattice generated by the simulation cell with periodic boundary condition. A uniform compensating background is added to enforce charge neutrality. The infinite sum over 𝑳s\boldsymbol{L}_{s} defines the Ewald interaction between a pair of point charges vE​(𝒓)v_{E}(\boldsymbol{r}) and the Madelung energy

vM≡lim𝒓→𝟎[vE​(𝒓)−1/r],v_{M}\equiv\lim_{\boldsymbol{r}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{0}}[v_{E}(\boldsymbol{r})-1/r], (13)

which is the Ewald potential of a single electron. Direct evaluation of the infinite lattice sum over 𝑳s\boldsymbol{L}_{s} is conditionally convergent, so a dual-space summation algorithm is typically used to evaluate the Ewald interaction

vE​(𝒓)=∑𝑳svs​r​(𝒓−𝑳s)+1Ω​∑𝑮s≠𝟎v𝑮sl​r−1Ω​lim𝑮→𝟎v𝑮s​r,\displaystyle v_{E}(\boldsymbol{r})=\sum\limits_{\boldsymbol{L}_{s}}v^{sr}(\boldsymbol{r}-\boldsymbol{L}_{s})+\dfrac{1}{\Omega}\sum\limits_{\boldsymbol{G}_{s}\neq\boldsymbol{0}}v^{lr}_{\boldsymbol{G}_{s}}-\dfrac{1}{\Omega}\lim\limits_{\boldsymbol{G}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{0}}v^{sr}_{\boldsymbol{G}}, (14)

where the Coulomb interaction is expressed as the sum of short-range vs​rv^{sr} and long-range vl​rv^{lr} pieces 1/r=vs​r​(r)+vl​r​(r)1/r=v^{sr}(r)+v^{lr}(r) with v𝑮s​rv^{sr}_{\boldsymbol{G}} and v𝑮l​rv^{lr}_{\boldsymbol{G}} being their Fourier transforms. In two spatial dimensions, we have the following concrete expressions: vGl​r=2​π/G​erfc​(G/(2​α))v^{lr}_{G}=2\pi/G~\text{erfc}(G/(2\alpha)), vs​r​(r)=1/r​erfc​(α​r)v^{sr}(r)=1/r~\text{erfc}(\alpha r) and lim𝑮→𝟎v𝑮s​r=2​π/α\lim\limits_{\boldsymbol{G}\rightarrow\boldsymbol{0}}v^{sr}_{\boldsymbol{G}}=2\sqrt{\pi}/\alpha, where α\alpha is a screening length in reciprocal space. 𝑮s\boldsymbol{G}_{s} is the reciprocal lattice of 𝑳s\boldsymbol{L}_{s}. More detailed analysis of the Coulomb interaction with periodic boundary conditions can be found in Refs. [42, 43].

The Hamiltonian can be simplified using Hartree atomic units. The Bohr radius is determined by the ratio of the constants aB=e24​π​ϵ/ℏ22​ma_{B}=\dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\epsilon}/\dfrac{\hbar^{2}}{2m} with a vacuum value of (e24​π​ℏ2)​meϵ0=0.529177210544\left(\dfrac{e^{2}}{4\pi\hbar^{2}}\right)~\dfrac{m_{e}}{\epsilon_{0}}=0.529177210544 Å. Using aBa_{B} as length units, eq. (11) becomes

H=Eh​(12​∇~i2+V~E),H=E_{h}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\tilde{\nabla}_{i}^{2}+\tilde{V}_{E}\right), (15)

where the Hartree energy Eh=ℏ2m​aB2E_{h}=\dfrac{\hbar^{2}}{ma_{B}^{2}} with a vacuum value of 27.2113862459827.21138624598 eV.

I.6 Wave Function Architectural Details

Our neural network backflow 𝒩{\mathcal{N}} is based on the message passing network proposed in [22]. The main idea is to iteratively update two streams of one- and two-body information 𝒉i(t)∈ℝd1\boldsymbol{h}^{(t)}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}} and 𝒉i​j(t)∈ℝd2\boldsymbol{h}^{(t)}_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}} for each electron ii and pair ii and jj, at each message passing layer t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T. In each layer tt, the two streams are combined with the “visible” features of the system, 𝒗i\boldsymbol{v}_{i} and 𝒗i​j\boldsymbol{v}_{ij}, to update the message, 𝒎i​j(t)\boldsymbol{m}^{(t)}_{ij}, between electron pair ii and jj.

𝒈i(t)=\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}^{(t)}_{i}= [𝒗i,𝒉i(t−1)],\displaystyle~\Big[\boldsymbol{v}_{i},\ \boldsymbol{h}^{(t-1)}_{i}\Big]\,, (16)
𝒈i​j(t)=\displaystyle\boldsymbol{g}^{(t)}_{ij}= [𝒗i​j,𝒉i​j(t−1)],\displaystyle~\Big[\boldsymbol{v}_{ij},\ \boldsymbol{h}^{(t-1)}_{ij}\Big]\,, (17)
𝒉i(t)=\displaystyle\boldsymbol{h}^{(t)}_{i}= ℱ1(t)​(∑j≠i𝒎i​j(t),𝒈i(t))+𝒉i(t−1),\displaystyle~{\mathcal{F}}_{1}^{(t)}\Big(\sum_{j\neq i}\boldsymbol{m}^{(t)}_{ij},\ \boldsymbol{g}^{(t)}_{i}\Big)+\boldsymbol{h}^{(t-1)}_{i}\,, (18)
𝒉i​j(t)=\displaystyle\boldsymbol{h}^{(t)}_{ij}= ℱ2(t)​(𝒎i​j(t),𝒈i​j(t))+𝒉i​j(t−1),\displaystyle~{\mathcal{F}}_{2}^{(t)}\Big(\boldsymbol{m}^{(t)}_{ij},\ \boldsymbol{g}^{(t)}_{ij}\Big)+\boldsymbol{h}^{(t-1)}_{ij}\,, (19)

where ℱh1(t){\mathcal{F}}_{h_{1}}^{(t)} and ℱh2(t){\mathcal{F}}_{h_{2}}^{(t)} are multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs). We include skip connections [44] to facilitate optimization. Here, we set 𝒉i(0)=h1\boldsymbol{h}_{i}^{(0)}=h_{1} and 𝒉i​j(0)=h2\boldsymbol{h}_{ij}^{(0)}=h_{2} for all ii and jj to ensure permutation equivariance, where h1h_{1} and h2h_{2} are optimizable vectors that are independent of ii and jj and initialized to zero.

In this work we choose the “visible” features as the following:

𝒗i=\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}_{i}= ∅,\displaystyle~\varnothing\,, (20)
𝒗i​j=\displaystyle\boldsymbol{v}_{ij}= [cos⁡(2​π​A−1​𝒓i​j),sin⁡(2​π​A−1​𝒓i​j),‖sin⁡(π​A−1​𝒓i​j)‖,si​j],\displaystyle~\Big[\cos(2\pi A^{-1} \bs{r}_{ij}),\ \sin(2\pi A^{-1} \bs{r}_{ij}),\ \norm{\sin(\pi A^{-1} \bs{r}_{ij})},\ s_{ij}\Big]\,, (21)

where AA is the cell tensor of the simulation box, 𝒓i​j=𝒓i−𝒓j\boldsymbol{r}_{ij}=\boldsymbol{r}_{i}-\boldsymbol{r}_{j} is the relative displacement between electron pair ii and jj, and si​j=2​δsi,sj−1s_{ij}=2\delta_{s_{i},s_{j}}-1 assigns +1+1 for parallel spins and −1-1 for antiparallel spins. We use the sine and cosine function as they are smooth and consistent with the periodic boundary condition [21]. Note that we take the one-body features 𝒗i\boldsymbol{v}_{i} to be empty to explicitly conserve the translational and time-reversal (spin-flipping) symmetry in the construction of neural network backflow 𝒩{\mathcal{N}}. Additional information such as sis_{i} and (periodic wrapped) 𝒓i\boldsymbol{r}_{i} can be included in 𝒗i\boldsymbol{v}_{i} to break the symmetry if desired.

The message 𝒎i​j(t)\boldsymbol{m}^{(t)}_{ij} is computed from another MLP ℱm(t){\mathcal{F}}_{m}^{(t)} that takes the two-body features 𝒈i​j(t)\boldsymbol{g}_{ij}^{(t)} as input, and is reweighted by an attention matrix 𝒜i​j(t){\mathcal{A}}^{(t)}_{ij} which itself is a function of 𝒈i​j(t)\boldsymbol{g}^{(t)}_{ij} from all electron pairs:

𝒎i​j(t)=\displaystyle\boldsymbol{m}^{(t)}_{ij}= 𝒜i​j(t)​({𝒈i​j(t)})⊙ℱm(t)​(𝒈i​j(t)),\displaystyle~{\mathcal{A}}_{ij}^{(t)}\Bigl(\Bqty{\bs{g}_{ij}^{(t)}}\Bigr)\odot{\mathcal{F}}_{m}^{(t)}\Big(\boldsymbol{g}_{ij}^{(t)}\Big)\,, (22)

where ⊙\odot denotes element-wise multiplication. The attention matrix 𝒜i​j(t){\mathcal{A}}_{ij}^{(t)} is computed with the particle attention mechanism proposed in [22] with modified scaling and an extra linear layer to facilitate training:

𝒜i​j(t)=\displaystyle{\mathcal{A}}_{ij}^{(t)}= Linear(t)∘GELU​(1N​∑lN𝒒i​l(t)​𝒌l​j(t)),\displaystyle~\mathrm{Linear}^{(t)}\circ\mathrm{GELU}\pqty{\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}} \sum_l^N \bs{q}_{il}^{(t)} \bs{k}_{lj}^{(t)}}\,, (23)
𝒒i​j(t)=\displaystyle\boldsymbol{q}_{ij}^{(t)}= Wq(t)⋅𝒈i​j(t),\displaystyle~W_{q}^{(t)}\cdot\boldsymbol{g}_{ij}^{(t)}\,, (24)
𝒌i​j(t)=\displaystyle\boldsymbol{k}_{ij}^{(t)}= Wk(t)⋅𝒈i​j(t),\displaystyle~W_{k}^{(t)}\cdot\boldsymbol{g}_{ij}^{(t)}\,, (25)

where Wq(t),Wk(t)∈ℝd2×d2W_{q}^{(t)},W_{k}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}\times d_{2}} are optimizable weight matrices that act on the feature dimension, and the attention mixes the information on the dimension of electron pairs. The “∘\circ” symbol represents function composition (i.e., (f∘g)​(x)=f⁡(g⁡(x))(f\circ g)(x)=f(g(x))).

All the MLPs denoted by ℱ{\mathcal{F}} (ℱ1(t){\mathcal{F}}_{1}^{(t)}, ℱ2(t){\mathcal{F}}_{2}^{(t)} and ℱm(t){\mathcal{F}}_{m}^{(t)}) contain a single hidden layer with GELU [45] activation function, i.e.,

ℱ=Linear2∘GELU∘Linear1.\displaystyle{\mathcal{F}}=\mathrm{Linear}_{2}\circ\mathrm{GELU}\circ\mathrm{Linear}_{1}\,. (26)

In addition, although not written explicitly in the equations, we apply layer normalization [46] to the inputs of all MLPs and attention layers (ℱ{\mathcal{F}} and 𝒜i​j{\mathcal{A}}_{ij}) to stabilize optimization.

After the message passing iterations, the backflow displacement 𝒩{\mathcal{N}} is computed by a linear transform from the final one-body stream 𝒉i(T)\boldsymbol{h}_{i}^{(T)}:

𝒙i=𝒓i+𝒩⁡({𝒓i})=𝒓i+Wbf⋅𝒉i(T).\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}_{i}=\boldsymbol{r}_{i}+{\mathcal{N}}(\{\boldsymbol{r}_{i}\})=\boldsymbol{r}_{i}+W_{\mathrm{bf}}\cdot\boldsymbol{h}_{i}^{(T)}\,. (27)

where Wbf∈ℝd1×2W_{\mathrm{bf}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times 2} is another weight matrix that maps the one-body stream to the displacement of electron ii in two dimensional space.

Similarly, the extra term 𝒰⁡({𝒓i}){\mathcal{U}}(\{\boldsymbol{r}_{i}\}) in the Jastrow factor is a sum of one-body contributions, which are computed from the final one-body stream 𝒉i(T)\boldsymbol{h}_{i}^{(T)} and the backflow wrapped coordinates 𝒙i\boldsymbol{x}_{i}:

𝒰⁡({𝒓i})=\displaystyle{\mathcal{U}}(\{\boldsymbol{r}_{i}\})= ∑i𝒥​(𝒉i(T),GELU∘Linearpre​(𝒙i)),\displaystyle~\sum_{i}{\mathcal{J}}\pqty{\bs{h}_i^{(T)},\ \mr{GELU} \circ\mr{Linear_{pre}}(\bs{x}_i)}\,, (28)
𝒥=\displaystyle{\mathcal{J}}= LinearL∘GELU∘⋯∘Linear1,\displaystyle~\mathrm{Linear}_{L}\circ\mathrm{GELU}\circ\cdots\circ\mathrm{Linear}_{1}\,, (29)

where Linearpre:ℝ2→ℝd1\mathrm{Linear_{pre}}:\ \mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}} is a linear layer that maps the wrapped coordinates 𝒙i\boldsymbol{x}_{i} to a vector of the same dimension as one-body stream 𝒉i\boldsymbol{h}_{i}, so that they have comparable contribution in the MLP. 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} is a MLP with L−1L-1 hidden layers that outputs a scalar. In practice, we use L=4L=4 for 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} (i.e., 3 hidden layers). We also apply skip connections between all the hidden layers of 𝒥{\mathcal{J}} to facilitate optimization.

In our calculations, we set the size of the hidden layers to 32 for all MLPs. We also set d1=32d_{1}=32 and d2=26d_{2}=26 so that the size of 𝒈i\boldsymbol{g}_{i} and 𝒈i​j\boldsymbol{g}_{ij} are equal to 32 as well. In addition, we choose the number of planewaves Nk=3​NN_{k}=3N where NN is the number of electrons (2​N2N for 120 electron systems) rounding to the nearest closed shell value. This results in a total number of parameters slightly less than 50,000 for calculations with 56 electrons, which can be easily handled by our implementation of stochastic reconfiguration (SR).

To summarize, our wavefunction ansatz largely follows the message passing network from [22], with the following major differences:

  • •

    We use a linear combination of planewaves for each single-particle orbital ϕa\phi_{a}, instead of a single planewave or Gaussian function, to allow for automatic detection of liquid and crystal phases.

  • •

    We employ a dedicated Jastrow factor term 𝒰{\mathcal{U}} that depends on both the one-body stream and the backflow coordinates, for better expressivity. We also include the standard pairwise term u2u_{2} to help capture the cusp condition.

  • •

    We apply skip connection and layer normalization as well as some smaller modifications to facilitate optimization.

I.7 Sampling and Optimization Details

We employ the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm (MALA) [32] to sample electron configurations from the unnormalized probability given by the trial wavefunction |ΨT|2\absolutevalue{\Psi_T}^{2}. Namely, at each step in the Markov chain, the new electron configuration R~\tilde{R} is proposed by the following formula:

R~=R+τ∇log|ΨT​(R)|2+2​τξ,\displaystyle\tilde{R}=R+\tau\gradient\log\absolutevalue{\Psi_T (R)}^{2}+\sqrt{2\tau}\xi, (30)

where RR is the current electron configuration and ξ\xi is a random variable drawn from the standard Gaussian distribution in 2​N2N dimension. The proposed sample is then accepted or rejected according to the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. The step size τ\tau is tuned adaptively during the optimization procedure to achieve a suitable acceptance rate.

In practice, we run 1024 Markov chains in parallel, so that we have a batch size of 1024 in the estimation of energy and gradients. To reduce auto-correlation, we run 20 MALA steps between each optimization step, and only use the electron configurations generated from the last step in the optimization. We increase or decrease the step size τ\tau by 10% every 10 optimization steps, to maintain the harmonic average of acceptance rate staying around 0.650.65. We also clip the individual components of the gradient to have a absolute value smaller than one, to stabilize the acceptance rate in the sampling process. In both liquid and crystal phases, the initial electron configurations are chosen to be close to the positions of Wigner crystals with a small Gaussian perturbation. We thermalize the samples with 2000 MALA steps before the optimization starts. We find it is hard to change the spin pattern in the crystal phase in sampling, since it is a rare event for two localized electrons to exchange their position. Therefore we employ two strategy in initializing the spin configurations: aligning with the antiferromagnetic (AFM) pattern in the Wigner crystal or fully random. We find no difference for the two in liquid phase. In crystal phase, the AFM initialization generally achieves lower energy while the random initialization often gets stuck in local minima.

The optimization is conducted with a modified version of stochastic reconfiguration (SR) algorithm named SPRING [35], which introduced an extra term, analogous to the momentum in stochastic gradient descent, to speed up convergence. Briefly speaking, the update of the parameters at step tt is given by

d​θt=\displaystyle d\theta_{t}= (S+λ​I)−1​(g+λ​μ​d​θt−1),\displaystyle~(S+\lambda I)^{-1}(g+\lambda\,\mu\,d\theta_{t-1})\,,
θt+1=\displaystyle\theta_{t+1}= θt−η​d​θt\displaystyle~\theta_{t}-\eta\,d\theta_{t} (31)

where θt\theta_{t} stands for the parameters at step tt. SS and gg are the quantum geometric (Fisher) matrix and gradients as in standard SR or natural gradient descent (NGD). η\eta is the learning rate, which is set to decay as a inverse function of tt, η=η0​(1+(t/T))−1\eta=\eta_{0}(1+(t/T))^{-1} with TT being the “delay” of the decay. λ\lambda and μ\mu are hyperparameters controlling the strength of damping and momentum decay. Setting λ=μ=0\lambda=\mu=0 will reduce the algorithm to standard SR without diagonal shift. Following the technique in KFAC [47], we also scale d​θtd\theta_{t} with a scalar so that its norm induced by the inverse Fisher matrix is smaller than a constant CC. To efficiently solve the matrix inversion, we take advantage of the sparsity of Fisher matrix SS when the number of samples is smaller than the number of parameters, and apply the the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury formula as described in Ref [48].

In practice, we set λ=0.001\lambda=0.001, μ=0.9\mu=0.9, T=1000T=1000 and C=η0C=\eta_{0}. The starting learning rate is chosen dependent on density to accommodate different energy scales, as η0={0.5,2,5}\eta_{0}=\{0.5,2,5\} for rs={5,10,15}r_{s}=\{5,10,15\}, η0=10\eta_{0}=10 for 15<rs≤3015<r_{s}\leq 30, and η0=15\eta_{0}=15 for rs>30r_{s}>30 except that η0={20,25,30}\eta_{0}=\{20,25,30\} for rs={35,36,50}r_{s}=\{35,36,50\}.

I.8 Visualizing the Optimized Wave Function

To better understand the final trained wave function ansatz, we can attempt to visualize certain components independently. Through these components, there are signs of the liquid to crystal transition. However, as we are not sampling the wave function distribution, and are ignoring the determinant and Jastrow factor, these signals may be potentially spurious.

First we observe the effects of the backflow 𝒩\mathcal{N} by following the effects of displacing a single electron along a path, shown in Fig. S7. For small rsr_{s}, such as shown in (a), there are strong corrections to the initial positions. For larger rsr_{s}, shown in (b) and (c) there is a much weaker effect and the electrons mostly remain at their initial positions, except when the displaced electron nears another electron. This matches the expected behavior seen in DMC, where backflow is essential to obtaining good liquid results at small to intermediate rsr_{s}.

As another demonstration of backflow correlations, instead of displacing a single electron a varied distance, is to displace the electron once a small amount Δ​r\Delta r and recursively call the backflow on the output positions

{rjo​u​t}=𝒩∘𝒩∘⋯∘𝒩({xjc⋅(1+Δrδ(r−r0)})),\{r^{out}_{j}\}=\mathcal{N}\circ\mathcal{N}\circ\dots\circ\mathcal{N}\left(\{x^{c}_{j}\cdot(1+\Delta r\delta(r-r_{0})\})\right), (32)

where {xjc}\{x^{c}_{j}\} have the electrons equi-spaced in a WC and r0r_{0} denotes the electron at the origin. After each application of 𝒩\mathcal{N}, the positions are always projected back into the unit cell. Shown in Fig. S8 are the final quasiparticle positions after a displacement of |Δ​r/rs|≈0.06|\Delta r/r_{s}|\approx 0.06 and iteratively applying backflow 𝒩\mathcal{N} to the resulting output 10 times. We see for small rsr_{s} (Fig. S8(a)), there is no apparent order to final positions. However for intermediate and large rsr_{s} (Fig. S8(b)-(c)), the output resembles the initial crystal positions having ‘corrected’ the defect. Note that the shift from the initial positions can be removed by removing the center of mass movement.

Then we can observe how the multi planewave coefficients ca​kσc_{ak}^{\sigma} are optimized across the different values of rsr_{s}, shown in Fig. S9. First, the norm is taken over the electron index aa then averaged over spins (σ={↑↓}\sigma=\{\uparrow\downarrow\}) such that |ck|=1/2∑σ(∑a|ca​kσ|2)1/2|c_{k}|=1/2\sum_{\sigma}(\sum_{a}|c_{ak}^{\sigma}|^{2})^{1/2}. In Fig. S9(a), each included kk value, a total of Nk=3​NN_{k}=3N, is plotted as an open circle, while the magnitude of |ck||c_{k}| is shown as the relative to the maximum value. For low to intermediate rsr_{s}, only those kk points around kFk_{F} are relatively strong although points further from kFk_{F} pick up weight as rsr_{s} increases. If we consider a threshold of |ck|≥O⁡(10−1)|c_{k}|\geq O(10^{-1}) as significant, in the liquid phase, less than 40%40\% of the kk points reach that threshold but in the crystal phase nearly all of them do. This can be seen in Fig. S9(b), where by radially averaging |ck||c_{k}|, as rsr_{s} increases the tail of the magnitudes at large |k||k| slowly increases, until all |ck||c_{k}| are roughly on the same order.
